sentences.text: [Name of our group, who we represent, and how many families we are in touch with.]

sections.heading: Why we are writing to you

sentences.text: We are writing because public records show that GRIN1-related neurodevelopmental disorder and SLC13A5-related epileptic encephalopathy are both linked to loss of function on the same broad disease mechanism path.

Public records also show high phenotype similarity between the two conditions, with overlap in encephalopathy, epileptic encephalopathy, reduced or abnormal eye contact, and abnormal nonverbal communication.
Because your community appears to have more developed natural history work and trial activity, we hope to learn from what you have already built.
Gene2Phenotype lists both GRIN1 and SLC13A5 disease links with definitive confidence.
Public records show that both conditions are currently curated as loss of function, although this is inferred.
A published literature search reports disease models for both genes, with 70 PubMed records for GRIN1 and 19 for SLC13A5.
Public records show active NIH-funded research in both areas in FY2025 to 2026.

sections.heading: What we would like to learn from or reuse

sentences.text: We would like to learn from your natural history study design, registry items, visit schedule, and consent approach.
We would also like to learn from your outcome measures and endpoints, because public records suggest the measured domains may overlap with ours.
Your clinical network, study sites, and investigators may also be relevant to families in our community.
We would welcome expert discussion about whether parts of your therapeutic strategy, assays, and trial design could inform GRIN1 work, while recognizing that this needs careful review first.
Public records also show an SLC13A5 natural history program in Citizen Health, formerly Ciitizen, that may offer practical ideas for data collection and family participation.
Public records show a named GRIN1 patient organization, CureGRIN Foundation, and we found no public record of a patient organization for SLC13A5 in the sources reviewed.
For GRIN1, public records show inclusion in Simons Searchlight, but we found no condition-specific GRIN1 registry or natural history study.
For SLC13A5, ClinicalTrials.gov records state there are two natural history studies, one in the United States and one remote only.
For GRIN1, public records show two pathway-level trials, but no trial that acts on the gene or its product.
For SLC13A5, a ClinicalTrials.gov record states there is a gene-level interventional study, NCT07102524.
We also know that GRIN1 must be treated with extra caution, because published claims report gain mechanisms as well as the curated loss-of-function mechanism.
Because of that, our two communities must not assume that the same treatment logic applies to every GRIN1 family.
The mechanism is recorded for the gene and condition, not for every family, so each family’s own GRIN1 variant needs confirmation by a clinical geneticist.
We also must not assume that a GRIN1 child could join an SLC13A5 trial, because public records do not assert eligibility across conditions and say families should ask the study team directly.
Even where there seems to be overlap, registry items, visit schedules, and outcome measures may differ if age of onset and severity differ between the conditions.
Do the age of onset and typical severity of SLC13A5-related disease match ours closely enough for its registry items and outcome measures to apply.
Which class does a given GRIN1 variant belong to: loss of function, gain of function, or dominant negative.
Has a child’s specific GRIN1 variant been functionally classified, and does it match the mechanism recorded for the condition.
What functional evidence exists for GRIN1, given that the curated mechanism is inferred from variant types rather than direct functional studies.
